name: Roman bridge
summary: A timber bridge across the Thames on the Fish Street Hill line, the reason the town stood here. A probable timber pier base of the late 1st century was excavated near Pudding Lane in 1981.
uncertainty: No bridge of the 50s is directly dated: a crossing 'in place by AD 63' is inferred from the layout of the quays, and a fixed bridge 'built by c. 85–90' is Milne's reading of the pier base, whose identification is still only probable. The exact line, pier count, deck height and the date it went out of use are unknown.

phases.label: First crossing (bridge or ferry; form conjectural)
phases.dateNote: Inference only; no structure of the 50s has been found.

phases.label: Timber bridge on pier bases
phases.dateNote: In place by c. 63 (inferred); pier base dated c. 85–90. End date unknown.

name: First forum and basilica
summary: The first civic centre on Cornhill: a gravelled court with a basilica about 40 × 20 m. It stayed in use while the much larger second forum was built around it.
uncertainty: Dated 'late 70s or 80s' (MOLA, after the 2025 Gracechurch Street discovery). Only the basilica size is documented; the court dimensions and all heights are conjecture.

phases.label: First forum and basilica
phases.dateNote: Built late 70s or 80s; taken down as the second forum was completed c. 120–125.

name: Second forum and basilica
summary: The great forum-basilica of Londinium, built around and over the first forum from about 100 CE; the basilica ran along its north side.
uncertainty: Plan known from scattered excavations. The c. 167 m square figure comes only from a secondary lead and was not verified; every height is conjecture. Marsden argues older models wrongly added inner porticoes and a cross-walkway (not shown here).

phases.label: Second forum-basilica
phases.dateNote: Built c. 100–125; ruinous or demolished in the early 300s.

name: Amphitheatre
summary: An oval arena beneath today's Guildhall Yard: built in timber about 74 CE and rebuilt shortly after 120 with a masonry arena wall and entrances. The seating was always timber.
uncertainty: Only the eastern end has been excavated. 'Over 100 m long' and a capacity of about 7,000 are the only verified figures; arena axes and seating height are estimates.

phases.label: Timber amphitheatre
phases.dateNote: c. 74 (MOLA).

phases.label: Rebuilt amphitheatre with masonry arena wall
phases.dateNote: Rebuilt shortly after 120; abandoned in the early to mid 4th century and then robbed.

name: Plantation Place fort
summary: An earth-and-timber fort of about 1.5 hectares built on Cornhill around 63 CE, soon after the Boudican revolt: the main physical evidence for the town's military-led recovery.
uncertainty: Known from one excavated corner; the rectangle shown is a schematic 1.5 ha outline, and the timber wall stands in for turf-and-timber ramparts about 3 m high. End date approximate.

name: Cripplegate fort
summary: A stone-walled fort of about 4.5 hectares on the north-west edge of the town, built about 120. It was probably out of use as a fort by the later 2nd century; its north and west walls were built into the city wall about 200.
uncertainty: Internal buildings are barely known and are not shown. The side lengths used (about 220 × 215 m) are unverified. The walls are shown standing until 200 although the garrison had probably gone decades earlier.

phases.label: Fort
phases.dateNote: Built c. 120; disused by the mid to late 2nd century.

name: City wall
summary: The landward wall, about 3 km long, 2–2.6 m thick and about 6.4 m high, built of Kentish ragstone c. 190–225 and enclosing some 134 hectares. It set the limits of the city for the next 1,400 years.
uncertainty: Condition between the 5th and 9th centuries is poorly documented; the weathered state shown is illustrative. Gate forms and tower spacing are schematic: the real eastern bastions are late Roman and the western ones medieval. The westward extension around Blackfriars (1282–1310) is not modelled.

phases.label: Roman wall
phases.dateNote: c. 190–225. Four original gates plus the fort's north gate (Cripplegate).

phases.label: Late Roman wall with Aldersgate added
phases.dateNote: Aldersgate is a later Roman insertion, c. 350 (date from a secondary lead only). Bastions were added to the eastern sector about the same time; they are not modelled.

phases.label: Wall reused by the Saxon and Norman city
phases.dateNote: Repaired repeatedly, notably in the 13th century.

phases.label: Late medieval wall with Moorgate
phases.dateNote: Moorgate opened 1415. Ludgate rebuilt 1586, Aldgate 1607–09, Aldersgate 1617 (rebuilds not separately modelled).

name: Riverside wall
summary: A wall about 1,700 m long added along the river front c. 255–275 on the line of Thames Street, closing the circuit. Its eastern end was strengthened as late as c. 388–402, parts still stood in the late 9th century, and it had gone by the 12th.
uncertainty: Its full line and the pace of its collapse are only partly known; the slow decay shown is illustrative.

name: Cannon Street riverside complex ('governor's palace')
summary: A large terraced riverside complex with courts and an ornamental pool under Cannon Street station, formerly called the governor's palace.
uncertainty: Its function, and whether it was one building at all, are disputed; the western range is entirely hypothetical and the c. 130 × 100 m extent is from secondary sources. The single symmetrical courtyard shown is a placeholder.

name: Huggin Hill baths
summary: A large public bath-house terraced into the hillside above the river.
uncertainty: Only 'late 1st century' could be verified for construction; demolition c. 180–200 is unverified. Elevation is reconstruction.

phases.label: Public baths
phases.dateNote: Late 1st century; demolition c. 180–200 (low confidence).

name: Temple of Mithras
summary: A small aisled temple on the east bank of the Walbrook, built c. 240–250 with its apse to the west; converted, probably to Bacchus, in the early 4th century. Found in 1954.
uncertainty: Roof form and height are reconstruction; the 18 × 8 m plan is from secondary sources.

phases.label: Temple of Mithras, later repurposed
phases.dateNote: Built c. 240–250 (coin dates); MOLA says it was used as a mithraeum for about 80 years and then repurposed, i.e. in the early 4th century. The building stood on; 380 is a modelling estimate for its end, not a dated end of worship.

name: Road to the bridge from the south (Borough High Street line)
summary: The approach road across the Southwark islands, where the roads from the Kent coast and the south met before the bridge.
uncertainty: Line simplified; the internal street grid was only partly regular.

name: Road north (Bishopsgate line)
summary: The road from the bridge past the forum and north towards Lincoln and York.
uncertainty: Use of the stretch inside the walls between the 5th and 9th centuries is uncertain. Line simplified; the internal street grid was only partly regular.

name: Main east–west Roman street
summary: The principal street of Londinium, running east–west north of the Walbrook crossing.
uncertainty: Line simplified; the internal street grid was only partly regular.

name: Cheapside – Cornhill
summary: The market street ('ceap') of the re-established Saxon city, the spine of the medieval street plan.
uncertainty: The date at which the late Saxon street grid was laid out is debated (late 9th to 10th century).

name: Road west (Holborn line)
summary: The Roman road west from Newgate towards Silchester, still a main road in 1625.
uncertainty: Line simplified; the internal street grid was only partly regular.

name: Fleet Street – Strand – King Street
summary: The road along the river terrace from Ludgate through Lundenwic to Westminster.
uncertainty: Probably of Roman origin, but that is not proven for its whole length.

name: Walbrook stream
summary: The stream that divided the Roman and medieval city. Progressively built over and culverted; gone from view by the late 16th century.
uncertainty: No single date exists for the covering; Stow (1598) describes it as wholly vaulted over. The gradual narrowing shown is illustrative.

phases.label: Open stream
phases.dateNote: Covered piecemeal from c. 1440; fully vaulted inside the walls by c. 1550–60.

name: River Fleet
summary: A tributary entering the Thames at Blackfriars; an open, increasingly foul river throughout this period.
uncertainty: It silted and narrowed from the 13th century; the constant width shown is a simplification.

name: St Paul's Cathedral
summary: A cathedral has stood on Ludgate Hill since 604. The medieval building, 'Old St Paul's', was one of the longest churches in Europe and carried a very tall timber spire until 1561.
uncertainty: Nothing is known of the form of the Anglo-Saxon churches; the small buildings shown before 1087 are placeholders. Overall length 586 ft (about 179 m) is documented. Published spire heights range from about 122 to 158 m (149 m is the traditional figure); the model uses about 144 m and no figure is a reliable measurement. The position of the crossing along the 179 m church (93 m from the west front, kept from the Romanesque church) is a modelling choice, not a measurement.

phases.label: Anglo-Saxon cathedral (form unknown)
phases.dateNote: Founded 604. No fabric or exact site of the Saxon church has been identified.

phases.label: Late Saxon cathedral (form unknown)
phases.dateNote: Rebuilt after the fire of 962; destroyed in the fire of 1087.

phases.label: Old St Paul's: Romanesque church under construction
phases.dateNote: Begun after the 1087 fire.

phases.label: Old St Paul's with spire
phases.dateNote: Steeple erected 1221/22.

phases.label: Old St Paul's extended east (the New Work, 1251–1314), with renewed spire
phases.dateNote: The Gothic 'New Work' east end was begun in 1251 (VCH) and the renewed spire dedicated in 1314, used here as the completion of the work (the 1314 date is not confirmed by the VCH pages read). Extension phase: the Romanesque church stands until then. Spire destroyed by lightning and fire, 4 June 1561. All phases from 1087 share the west front (89.5 m west of the landmark point), so the New Work extends the church eastwards, and the crossing tower stays where the Romanesque church has it (93 m from the west front).

phases.label: Old St Paul's without its spire
phases.dateNote: Roofs repaired 1561–66; the spire was never rebuilt. Tower stump about 62 m.

name: Queenhithe
summary: A trading shore from the late 880s ('Æthelred's Hythe', first charter 889): at first an open beach market, with low timber revetments from the late 10th century and embankments dated 1021 and 1045. The main dock above the bridge through the Middle Ages.

phases.label: Revetted dock
phases.dateNote: Revetments late 10th century; embankments tree-ring dated 1021 and 1045.

uncertainty: The beach-market phase (c. 886-970) had no built quay and is not modelled. The dock is drawn as an open inlet in the reclaimed frontage (site.river.inlets 'queenhithe-inlet'): its head is put at the model's waterline of about 1000, where this landmark stands, and its 34 m width, the hard, sheds and hoist are generic, not surveyed.

name: Late Saxon and Norman timber bridge
summary: A timber bridge existed again by about 1000 CE and was repaired or rebuilt several times before the stone bridge replaced it.
uncertainty: Its form and the number of rebuildings are not known; the model is generic. Line: drawn parallel to the stone bridge and about 33 m downstream (east) of it along its whole length. The side follows the account that the timber bridge stayed in use just downstream while the stone bridge was built beside it (Stow; Watson, LAMAS Transactions 50, as summarised in this project's research notes); a later tradition (Old and New London) puts it further east still, from Botolph's wharf. The distance is not documented: 33 m is chosen so that it clears the stone bridge's downstream starlings and chapel pier (which rose while the timber bridge was in use) and lands east of St Magnus at the City end. The definitive account (Watson, Brigham and Dyson 2001, MoLAS Monograph 8) is not open access and was not checked; its line may differ.

phases.label: Successive timber bridges (one destroyed by the storm of 1091)
phases.dateNote: A bridge existed by about 1000. London Museum records its destruction by a storm in 1091; when it was rebuilt is not recorded, so this phase stands for successive bridges, not one structure. The 1014 'pulling down' is saga tradition only. Burned in 1135 or 1136 depending on the source.

phases.label: Rebuilt timber bridge
phases.dateNote: Last timber rebuild 1163 (Peter of Colechurch); replaced by the stone bridge built alongside.

name: Old London Bridge
summary: The stone bridge of 19 arches and a drawbridge opening, begun in 1176 and finished in 1209, about 276 m long and only about 6 m wide, lined with houses, with a chapel on its central pier and a fortified gate at the Southwark end.
uncertainty: Length 276 m follows MOLA (the traditional figure is 926 ft, about 282 m). The deck height above the water is undocumented and the 8 m used is an assumption. Individual pier, arch and starling sizes are generated, not measured. Five arches collapsed in the winter of 1281–82 and two (with the Stone Gate) in January 1437; those repairs are not animated.

name: Houses on London Bridge
summary: Houses stood on the bridge from soon after it was finished: about 140 by 1358 and about 130 in the 16th century, overhanging the river on both sides of a roadway only about 4 m wide and bridging it in places.
uncertainty: No house is individually documented before the 16th–17th century views, and those disagree in detail. Number of storeys before the 15th century is conjectural.

phases.label: First houses
phases.dateNote: Destroyed in the fire of 11 July 1212.

name: Chapel of St Thomas on the Bridge
summary: A two-storey chapel on the large central pier, dedicated to Thomas Becket. Rebuilt 1387–96; closed in 1548 and turned into a house, shop and warehouse.

phases.label: Rebuilt chapel
phases.dateNote: Rebuilt 1387–96.

phases.label: Chapel converted to a dwelling
phases.dateNote: Chapel closed 1548; converted to a house in 1549 (first lease 1553 in another account).

uncertainty: Dimensions are not documented; the form follows later views.

name: Great Stone Gate
summary: The fortified gate at the Southwark end of the bridge. After 1577 the heads of traitors were displayed here.

phases.label: Stone gate
phases.dateNote: Collapsed with two arches in January 1437.

phases.label: Rebuilt stone gate
phases.dateNote: Rebuilt after the collapse of January 1437 (completion about 1466); burned in Fauconberg's attack of 1471 and repaired.

phases.label: Rebuilt stone gate with traitors' heads
phases.dateNote: Traitors' heads were shown on the Drawbridge Gate until it was taken down in April 1577 (Stow 1633, via MoEML) and from then on over the gate at the Southwark end.

uncertainty: Dimensions undocumented.

name: Drawbridge Gate
summary: A gate tower beside the drawbridge, seventh opening from the Southwark end. Demolished in 1577 and replaced by Nonsuch House.

phases.label: Drawbridge tower
phases.dateNote: Early form poorly documented.

uncertainty: Dimensions undocumented. Traitors' heads were displayed on this tower until its demolition in 1577.

name: Nonsuch House
summary: A four-and-a-half-storey timber house with corner turrets and onion domes, built across the bridge in 1577–79 on the site of the drawbridge tower; its design is attributed to Lewis Stockett, Surveyor of the Queen's Works.
uncertainty: Footprint about 22.9 × 7.6 m in the Gerhold-based account; height undocumented, and no measured contemporary drawing exists. It is said by later tradition, unverified, to have been prefabricated in the Netherlands.

phases.label: Nonsuch House
phases.dateNote: Tower taken down 1577; house finished September 1579 (Stow).

name: London Bridge waterworks
summary: Tide-driven waterwheels under the northernmost arches, set up by Peter Morris in 1581–82 to pump river water into the city.

phases.label: Waterwheels
phases.dateNote: Operational 1582 (Stow). Corn mills were added at the south end c. 1590–91 (not modelled).

name: St Magnus the Martyr
summary: The parish church at the north end of the bridge; every traveller crossing passed its door.
uncertainty: No firm earliest mention could be verified: 1067 rests on a suspect charter, so 'by the early 12th century' is used. No reliable image of the medieval building survives; the form and the date of enlargement are generic.

name: Fishmongers' Hall
summary: The riverside hall of the Fishmongers' Company, just upstream of the bridge, from 1434.
uncertainty: 1434 is the traditional date of acquisition and was not verified. Appearance before the 1640s views is conjectural.

name: St Olave, Southwark
summary: Church at the south bridge foot dedicated to St Olaf of Norway, in existence by the late 11th century.
uncertainty: In existence by the late 11th century; the medieval form is generic.

phases.label: Church
phases.dateNote: In existence by the late 11th century: probably the church recorded in Domesday (1086) and first named in 1096. 1070 is a display anchor, not a construction date; a pre-Conquest origin is possible but not established by the sources read.

name: St Mary Overie (St Saviour's)
summary: A minster recorded in Domesday (1086), refounded in 1106 as an Augustinian priory at the Southwark bridge foot and rebuilt in Gothic style after the fire of 1212. It became the parish church of St Saviour in 1540 and survives as Southwark Cathedral.

phases.label: Minster recorded in Domesday (form unknown)
phases.dateNote: The first written reference is a 'minster' in Domesday Book (1086); in 1106 the church was refounded as an Augustinian priory (Southwark Cathedral). Its form is unknown and the small church shown is a placeholder; 1086 is the date of the record, not of building.

phases.label: Norman priory church
phases.dateNote: Refounded 1106; burned 11 July 1212 in the same fire as the bridge.

phases.label: Church with heightened tower
phases.dateNote: The two upper stages of the tower were built in 1520–28 (VCH Surrey), shown as an extension rising while the earlier church stands. Priory surrendered 27 October 1539; parish church of St Saviour from 1540.

name: Winchester Palace
summary: The London house of the bishops of Winchester on Bankside, with a great hall whose rose-window gable still stands.

phases.label: Bishop's palace
phases.dateNote: Henry of Blois, c. 1140s.

phases.label: Palace with great hall
phases.dateNote: The standing great hall is a 14th-century rebuild.

name: Billingsgate
summary: The dock and market below the bridge, in use by about 1000 CE.
uncertainty: Drawn as an open inlet in the reclaimed frontage (site.river.inlets 'billingsgate-inlet'). The head is put at the model's waterline of about 990, at the foot of the lane to the dock (this landmark's point, moved 33 m north from the middle of the old hard for that reason); the 30 m width, the hard, sheds and hoist are generic, not surveyed.

name: Roman quays and warehouses
summary: Massive oak-timber quays with open-fronted warehouses behind, rebuilt further out into the river several times between the 1st and 3rd centuries.
uncertainty: The model shows one generalised quay line that follows the modelled bank; the real sequence had several distinct waterfronts advancing about 35 m in all (a secondary figure). Warehouses are generic.

phases.label: First timber revetment
phases.dateNote: Tree-ring date 52 CE.

phases.label: Timber quays and warehouses
phases.dateNote: Tree-ring anchors: great quay 63, landing stage c. 70, extension 102, further advances to the mid 3rd century; quays dismantled by the 4th century.

name: Westminster Abbey
summary: A small Benedictine monastery stood here from about 960; its buildings are not reconstructed. Edward the Confessor's great church, consecrated in 1065, was replaced from 1245 by Henry III's Gothic abbey. The new nave was built westwards from 1376 and finished in 1517; the west towers were not built until the 18th century and are not shown.
uncertainty: The Confessor's church is known from excavation and the Bayeux Tapestry; its elevation is reconstruction. The plan is schematic: the 156 m overall length (Abbey plus Henry VII's Chapel) is split between the two landmarks, the east end is pinned where the chapel joins and the west front falls where that length puts it; neither end is surveyed here.

phases.label: Henry III's abbey: east end, transepts and part of the nave
phases.dateNote: By 1269 only the east end, transepts and first nave bays were finished; the Romanesque nave stood for another century. The east end is pinned 60 m east of the landmark point, where Henry VII's Chapel (its own landmark) later joins it; the nave rebuilt from 1376 shares it.

phases.label: Abbey with the nave rebuilt westwards (1376–1517)
phases.dateNote: Work on the new nave resumed in 1376 and was finished in 1517 (Westminster Abbey). An extension phase: Henry III's church with the old Romanesque nave stays standing while the new nave rises, and is replaced only when the nave is complete. No west towers before 1745. Drawn 124 m long from the east end it shares with Henry III's church, so the new work rises at the west: the 156 m used before is the Abbey's length including Henry VII's Chapel, which is its own 32 m landmark east of it (the two models had double-counted it). The crossing is kept where Henry III's church has it.

name: Henry VII's Lady Chapel
summary: The Perpendicular Lady Chapel at the east end of Westminster Abbey.

phases.label: Lady Chapel
phases.dateNote: Consecrated 19 February 1516.

name: Westminster Hall and Palace
summary: William II's great hall of 1097–99, the largest in England, given its hammerbeam roof in the 1390s. The royal palace grew around it.
uncertainty: The surrounding palace buildings are shown only as a generic range. The 73 × 20.5 m plan was seen only in secondary summaries; wall and roof heights are estimates.

phases.label: Hall heightened and given its hammerbeam roof
phases.dateNote: Roof commissioned 1393; the Norman walls were kept, heightened and refaced to carry it. A Commons debate of 1914 gives the work as 1393–1402; the lanterns are usually dated 1397–98 and work stopped in 1401 with decoration unfinished. 1399 is an approximate display anchor for substantial completion, not a documented date. Extension phase: the Norman hall stays standing until then.

name: Tower of London: the White Tower
summary: William the Conqueror's great stone keep in the south-east corner of the Roman walls, begun in the 1070s and complete by about 1100.

phases.label: White Tower
phases.dateNote: Begun c. 1075–81, complete by c. 1100; 27 m to the battlements. Whitewashed from 1240.

uncertainty: The turrets' onion-shaped caps date from the early 1530s; the model shows one form throughout.

name: Tower of London: inner curtain wall
summary: The towered inner curtain built mainly under Henry III.
uncertainty: Wall line simplified to a quadrilateral.

phases.label: Inner curtain
phases.dateNote: Henry III, 1238–1240s. A first stone enclosure and ditch of c. 1190 is not shown.

name: Tower of London: outer curtain and moat
summary: Edward I's outer curtain wall and moat, 1275–85, which gave the Tower its concentric form.
uncertainty: Wall line simplified to a quadrilateral; the moat (about 50 m wide) is not modelled.

name: Baynard's Castle (first)
summary: A Norman castle in the south-west corner of the city, demolished in 1213; the site passed to the Blackfriars.
uncertainty: Its plan and appearance are unknown. A generic small keep is shown. Slighted 1213; the site was absorbed by Blackfriars in 1276. Nearby Montfichet's Tower, equally undocumented, is not shown.

name: Baynard's Castle (riverside house)
summary: A great riverside house rebuilt after a fire in 1428 and remodelled as a royal residence by Henry VII about 1501.

phases.label: Riverside mansion
phases.dateNote: A 14th-century riverside house preceded it; rebuilt after the fire of 1428.

name: Temple Church
summary: The Knights Templar's church with its round nave, consecrated in 1185; the chancel was added by 1240.

phases.label: Round church with hall chancel
phases.dateNote: The chancel was added east of the round nave (consecrated 1240); both phases pin the junction with the round, so the extension grows eastwards only.

name: Blackfriars
summary: The Dominican friary built from 1276 between Ludgate and the river; the city wall was moved west to enclose it. Dissolved 1538; its church was pulled down and the buildings became houses and, later, an indoor playhouse.
uncertainty: Layout is schematic.

phases.label: Dominican friary
phases.dateNote: Site granted 1276; church begun 1279 and built into the 1290s.

phases.label: Converted precinct (church demolished)
phases.dateNote: Surrendered 12 November 1538 (VCH); the church was demolished afterwards, in years these sources do not fix, so 1538 is the institutional, not the physical, boundary. Theatres in the former precinct: Blackfriars I from 1576 and Blackfriars II from 1596, distinct venues (EMLoT); the King's Men used the second from 1608–09.

name: Greyfriars (Christ Church)
summary: The Franciscan friary by Newgate. Its great 14th-century church, about 90 m long, became the parish church of Christ Church after the Dissolution.

phases.label: First friary
phases.dateNote: Drawn in the place of the great church's choir (its east end pinned to the great church's), since parts of the first church were taken into the new choir. Its exact plan is not known.

phases.label: Great church
phases.dateNote: Foundation stone of the great church laid 1306, finished 1327 (VCH; a chronicler says it was still not dedicated in 1357). VCH gives 300 × 89 ft; the 64 ft height is from another account. Parts of the first church were taken into the new choir, so the first friary stays standing while the great church rises (extension phase). Surrendered 12 November 1538; kept as Christ Church parish church from 1547.

name: Austin Friars
summary: The Augustinian friary founded in 1253. After 1538 the nave was given to London's Dutch Protestant community (1550).

phases.label: Nave only (Dutch Church)
phases.dateNote: Choir and steeple taken down around 1600. The nave kept is the west part of the rebuilt church: its west end is pinned to that church's west front.

name: Holy Trinity Priory, Aldgate
summary: A rich Augustinian priory founded in 1108 just inside Aldgate; the first London house to be dissolved (1532), then largely pulled down for a mansion.

phases.label: Priory
phases.dateNote: Founded 1107/08; burned 1132 and rebuilt; surrendered July 1531 (Stow) or 1532. VCH: surrendered February 1532 and granted to Lord Audley in 1534; when the church was pulled down is not established by the sources read, so the end shown is the surrender.

name: St Bartholomew's Priory and Hospital
summary: Founded by Rahere in 1123 beside Smithfield. After the Dissolution the nave was demolished and the choir kept as a parish church.

phases.label: Priory church (surrendered 1539)
phases.dateNote: Surrendered in October 1539 (VCH). The nave was then demolished and the choir kept as the parish church (Great St Bartholomew); the sources do not give the year of demolition, so 1543 is a display boundary, not continued monastic life.

phases.label: Choir only (parish church)
phases.dateNote: The choir kept as the parish church: its east end is pinned to the priory church's east end.

name: Charterhouse
summary: A Carthusian monastery founded in 1371 with a great cloister of individual cells; disbanded in 1538, a courtier's mansion from 1546 and Sutton's Hospital from 1611.

phases.label: Carthusian monastery (community disbanded 1538)
phases.dateNote: Founded 1371 on the plague cemetery of 1349; the cells took about 60 years to complete. Surrendered 10 June 1537 and formally disbanded 15 November 1538 (VCH). The buildings then stood, divided among Crown grantees, used as a royal storehouse from 1542 and largely derelict, until they were sold to Sir Edward North on 14 April 1546; the monastic community did not continue after 1538.

phases.label: Mansion, later Sutton's Hospital
phases.dateNote: Sir Edward North bought the site on 14 April 1546 and made a mansion of it; Sutton's Hospital from 1611.

name: Savoy Palace, later Savoy Hospital
summary: John of Gaunt's palace on the Strand, the grandest noble house in England, destroyed in the Peasants' Revolt of 1381. Henry VII's hospital was built on the ruins from 1505.
uncertainty: No reliable image of the palace exists; the model is generic.

phases.label: Savoy Palace
phases.dateNote: Peter of Savoy's house from 1245–46; Lancastrian palace of the 1350s; burned 1381 and left a ruin.

phases.label: Savoy Hospital
phases.dateNote: Stow gives only 'about 1509'; the completion date was not verified.

name: Guildhall
summary: The city's great hall, rebuilt from 1411, standing over the buried Roman amphitheatre.
uncertainty: An earlier stone guildhall stood on the site from the 12th–13th century; it is not shown.

phases.label: Great Hall
phases.dateNote: Begun 1411. The City of London gives 1411–1440 for the building, and the Gresham lecture a wider civic campaign of about 1411–1450 including the precinct. The hall is shown complete only at the end of the City's range; its exact completion year is not recorded in these sources.

name: Leadenhall
summary: A quadrangular public granary and market built in the 1440s on the site of the Roman basilica.

phases.label: Garner and market
phases.dateNote: Simon Eyre's quadrangle of the 1440s; damaged by fire in 1484.

name: Royal Exchange
summary: Thomas Gresham's bourse, built 1566–68 around an arcaded courtyard on the Antwerp model and named the Royal Exchange after Elizabeth I's visit in 1571.

phases.label: Gresham's Exchange
phases.dateNote: First brick 7 June 1566, slated November 1567; named 'Royal' at Elizabeth's visit of 23 January 1571.

uncertainty: No dimensions were found; the footprint is estimated.

name: Bridewell Palace
summary: Henry VIII's brick palace beside the Fleet, built 1515–23; given to the City in 1553 as a workhouse and prison.

name: York Place, later Whitehall Palace
summary: The archbishops of York's London house, seized by Henry VIII in 1529–30 and expanded into the largest palace in Europe, a sprawl of courts and galleries between the river and St James's Park.
uncertainty: Shown as generic courtyards; the real plan was irregular. The 'Holbein Gate' (c. 1531–32) and tiltyard are not separately modelled.

name: Banqueting House, Whitehall
summary: Inigo Jones's Palladian hall of 1619–22, the first fully classical building in London. It replaced a banqueting house of 1606–07 that burned in January 1619.

phases.label: Jacobean banqueting house
phases.dateNote: Built 1606–07 (opened January 1608), 120 × 53 ft; burned 12 January 1619.

phases.label: Inigo Jones's Banqueting House
phases.dateNote: 110 × 55 × 55 ft over a 16 ft undercroft; originally faced in three different stones.

name: Somerset House
summary: Protector Somerset's Renaissance palace on the Strand, 1547–52; Denmark House under James I's queen.

name: Northampton House (Suffolk House from 1614)
summary: A Jacobean courtyard mansion with corner turrets at Charing Cross, built about 1605–09 for the Earl of Northampton; known as Northumberland House only later.
uncertainty: Strand front about 162 ft (49 m); depth and height are estimates.

name: Lambeth Palace
summary: The London residence of the archbishops of Canterbury since about 1200, on the marshy bank opposite Westminster.

phases.label: Archbishop's house and chapel
phases.dateNote: Archbishop Baldwin acquired the site in 1189–90; the new palace was begun under Archbishop Langton (1207–29) and the chapel appears to be of the mid 13th century (RCHME). The 1200 start and the 1250 completion are approximate display anchors, not documented dates.

phases.label: Palace with Morton's Tower
phases.dateNote: Morton's Tower (the gatehouse) built by Cardinal Morton in 1490 (RCHME).

uncertainty: Dates here are from general reference knowledge and were not checked against a fetched source in this research pass.

name: Bermondsey Abbey
summary: A Cluniac priory (later abbey) founded in 1082 on the Bermondsey eyot; dissolved 1538 and replaced by a mansion.

phases.label: Priory
phases.dateNote: Founded in 1082 (Southwark Heritage). The 1140 completion and the 1538 demolition are not supported by a source read here: 1538 is the dissolution, and when the church was actually pulled down for Bermondsey House is not established.

uncertainty: Dates here are from general reference knowledge and were not checked against a fetched source in this research pass.

name: Custom House
summary: The quay where duties were collected. A custom house stood at Wool Quay by 1377 and John Churchman built a new one in 1382.

phases.label: Custom house at Wool Quay
phases.dateNote: In existence by 1377; Churchman's building 1382.

uncertainty: Sources conflict on an Elizabethan rebuilding: the Survey of London (vol. 15) says Churchman's house lasted until 1559, when it was superseded by a new custom house built under William Paulet, Marquess of Winchester, while a Gresham College lecture says Winchester's 1558 plan for a new custom house was never carried out. Until this is resolved the model shows one generic building throughout.

name: The Steelyard
summary: The walled riverside base of the Hanseatic merchants, with its guildhall and warehouses. Its privileges were withdrawn in 1598 but the buildings stood.

phases.label: Hanse compound
phases.dateNote: Guildhall of the German merchants by 1259; enlarged 1475; closed 1598, returned to the Hanse towns 1606.

uncertainty: Position estimated: Stow puts the Steelyard on Thames Street east of Cosin Lane, and MoEML south of Thames Street on the north bank, on the site later taken by Cannon Street station (1853). The compound is placed between the modelled Thames Street and the waterfront, with its long side parallel to the street (moved about 45 m south in the corrections of 14 November 2026, when it was found lying across the street line). Footprint generic.

name: The Rose playhouse
summary: Philip Henslowe's playhouse of 1587, the first on Bankside; its foundations were excavated in 1989.

phases.label: Enlarged playhouse
phases.dateNote: Enlarged 1591–92; out of use by about 1603 and gone by 1606.

uncertainty: Plan (14-sided, about 22 m) is from excavation; height is not documented.

name: The Swan playhouse
summary: Built about 1595 in Paris Garden; the subject of the only surviving sketch of an Elizabethan playhouse interior.
uncertainty: Size and number of sides are not documented; the model borrows the Globe estimate.

name: The Globe
summary: Built in 1599 from the timbers of the Theatre; burned on 29 June 1613 and rebuilt with a tiled roof by 1614.
uncertainty: Only a small arc of the foundations has been excavated: the roughly 30 m diameter and 20 sides are extrapolations (16–18 sides is also argued). Height is undocumented.

name: Bear Garden, later the Hope
summary: A baiting ring on Bankside, replaced in 1613–14 by the Hope, a dual-purpose playhouse and baiting house.

phases.label: Bear-baiting ring
phases.dateNote: Baiting rings on Bankside from the 1540s.

uncertainty: Sizes are estimates. Hollar's 1647 view swaps the labels of the Hope and the Globe.

name: City waterfront
summary: The built-up river frontage of the City: successive timber and later stone revetments pushed the bank out into the Thames, creating wharves between Thames Street and the water.
uncertainty: The model draws one continuous frontage that follows the modelled bank line. The real waterfront was a patchwork of separately owned wharves, inlets and stairs, and the pace of medieval reclamation is not reliably quantified.

name: Bankside and Southwark river wall
summary: The embanked south shore from Paris Garden past Winchester Palace to the bridge foot and St Olave's.
uncertainty: Dates of embankment are generalised; the line follows the modelled bank.

name: Roman shipping
summary: Three Roman vessels have been excavated in London: the Blackfriars ship (a flat-bottomed Romano-Celtic sailing barge that sank with Kentish ragstone about AD 150), the New Guy's House river barge (abandoned about AD 200) and the County Hall ship (a sea-going ship of Mediterranean build that sank after 293). The harbour was maintained to about AD 250, its quays were dismantled in the later 3rd century and the riverside wall then cut the town off from the river, so the traffic shown thins after 250 and again after 300. No Roman warship is evidenced at London. The vessel TYPES are dated and sourced individually (open a type in docs/VESSELS.md or data/locations/london/vessels.json); the number of craft and where each lies are illustrative, so this entry's own evidence class, which describes the placements, is conjectural.
uncertainty: Each vessel type rests on one excavated find; small boats and ferries are inferred. Numbers, positions and the split between quays and mid-stream moorings are illustrative.

phases.label: First ships at the new port
Barges, lighters and sea-going ships at the quays
phases.dateNote: Quays were built from about AD 62-3 and the harbour was maintained to about 250.

phases.label: Harbour no longer maintained
phases.dateNote: Quays dismantled in the later 3rd century; the County Hall ship sank after 293.

phases.label: Behind the riverside wall
phases.dateNote: Thinned to almost nothing; Roman rule in Britain ends about 410.

name: River traffic, late Saxon to Jacobean
summary: The river traffic of the walled city, changing with the evidence: clinker cargo ships with side rudders from the late Saxon revival; ships with castles and stern rudders from about 1200 and Hanseatic cogs from the 13th century; the clinker river barge called a shout in the 14th-15th centuries; carvel-built carracks below the bridge once the drawbridge was no longer raised (about 1500); then armed merchantmen in the Pool, hoys, lighters, Gravesend tilt-boats, western barges and the wherries of the watermen (Stow counted above 2,000 small boats in 1598). Sea-going ships lie below the bridge after 1500, oared craft everywhere. The vessel TYPES are dated and sourced individually (open a type in docs/VESSELS.md or data/locations/london/vessels.json); the number of craft and where each lies are illustrative, so this entry's own evidence class, which describes the placements, is conjectural.
uncertainty: Before about 1500 tall ships could pass the drawbridge to Queenhithe and the Steelyard, so a few are shown above the bridge. Numbers stand for a busy river without claiming a count; positions, headings and the mix within each phase are illustrative. Types not shown, because their dates or forms could not be verified: hulks as a distinct type, Peter boats, dung boats and the Dutch eel ships.

phases.label: Late Saxon revival
phases.dateNote: Alfred's restoration of the walled city in the 880s; Queenhithe and Billingsgate from the 10th century; Billingsgate tolls c. 1000.

phases.label: Castles and stern rudders appear
phases.dateNote: Ipswich seal (1200): earliest stern-post rudder; side rudders still drawn into the early 14th century.

phases.label: Last years of the drawbridge
phases.dateNote: The drawbridge was damaged by raising in 1481 and judged too dangerous by 1497.

phases.label: Carracks below the bridge, wherries above it
The crowded river of the panoramas

name: Logboats (illustrative)
summary: Before the Romans almost no craft are evidenced in this reach. Logboats (dugouts) are known from the Thames and its marshes, at Erith and upriver at Bourne End, so two are shown drawn up on the shore; sewn-plank boats such as the Dover boat are coastal and none is known from the Thames. The vessel TYPES are dated and sourced individually (open a type in docs/VESSELS.md or data/locations/london/vessels.json); the number of craft and where each lies are illustrative, so this entry's own evidence class, which describes the placements, is conjectural.
uncertainty: No logboat has been found between Westminster and the Tower, and the Thames finds are undated or dated only by period. The two boats stand for a sparse, unrecorded local use of the river; their number, place and dates are invented.

phases.label: Logboats on the shore
phases.dateNote: From the start of the period attributed to the nearest Thames logboat (Bourne End: Bronze or Iron Age, 2350 BCE-42 CE); no dated find in this reach allows a narrower window.

name: Boats at the Lundenwic shore (illustrative)
summary: Middle Saxon London (Lundenwic) traded by ship along the Strand, 'the beach', from about 600 until its abandonment by the 880s; wattle and timber embankments have been excavated, but no boat. Clinker-built traders and small boats are shown drawn up on the foreshore. In these centuries nothing is shown at the old Roman bridgehead, where no craft are evidenced. The vessel TYPES are dated and sourced individually (open a type in docs/VESSELS.md or data/locations/london/vessels.json); the number of craft and where each lies are illustrative, so this entry's own evidence class, which describes the placements, is conjectural.
uncertainty: The boats follow the Graveney boat (c. 895, Kent) and the clinker tradition; whether they carried sails is not known. Their number and place are invented.

phases.label: Traders and small boats on the Strand shore
phases.dateNote: Settlement from about 650; first recorded Viking raid 842; abandoned by the 880s.

name: Olaf's ships at the bridge (saga tradition)
summary: Longships below the timber bridge, standing for the saga account of an attack on London Bridge in 1014. The ships are drawn as Scandinavian longships of the period (Skuldelev 5 and Skuldelev 2 types, c. 1030-1042: clinker hulls, side rudders, single square sails, here furled while they row).
uncertainty: The attack is known only from Norse verse and a saga written about 200 years later; the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle is silent. Number, position and form of the ships are invented for the staging (conjectural), and the bridge is deliberately not shown collapsing.

phases.label: Ships below the bridge
phases.dateNote: Shown for 1014 only.
